broad.question: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: Mechanically derived short-range order and its impact on the multi-principal-element alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding of the paper that strain-induced MSRO forms along slip bands at cryogenic temperatures, and extends it by proposing that the pre-existing chemical order (CSRO) can precondition the microstructural evolution during deformation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis connects controllable thermal pre-treatment (annealing) to subsequent MSRO network formation and fracture toughness, thereby providing a processing-to-property link not addressed in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Tailoring the initial CSRO level via subcritical annealing can control the evolution and connectivity of mechanically induced SRO (MSRO) during cryogenic deformation, which in turn governs toughness retention in high‐entropy alloys.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An fcc high‐entropy alloy (Fe40Mn40Cr10Co10) that has been thermally processed to exhibit either a low or a moderately high level of diffusion‐mediated CSRO, achieved by varying the annealing temperature/time (e.g., compare rapid water‐quenched versus furnace‐cooled after ageing at ~773 K).
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal pre-treatment to produce distinct initial CSRO levels, then subject specimens to identical quasistatic tensile deformation at 77 K.
hypothesis.conditions: Deformation is performed at 77 K under quasistatic strain rates that avoid significant diffusion, with the only variable being the pre-deformation CSRO state established by tailored annealing.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The distribution, size, and connectivity of MSRO domains that form along slip bands upon deformation.
hypothesis.mechanism: A higher pre-existing CSRO level can lower the nucleation barrier for MSRO formation upon deformation, leading to a finer and more interconnected MSRO network along the slip bands. This network is hypothesized to act as a barrier to crack initiation and propagation by diffusing local stress concentrations at the microscale. Conversely, a low initial CSRO state may lead to less uniform MSRO formation, giving rise to localized stress concentrations and inferior toughness retention.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Samples with higher initial CSRO are predicted to exhibit a more refined, interconnected MSRO distribution (as seen via TEM/FFT analysis) and higher fracture toughness (e.g., increased KIC or higher Charpy energy absorption) than those with low initial CSRO when deformed under otherwise identical conditions.
hypothesis.baseline: HEA samples with minimal initial CSRO produced by rapid quenching, whose deformation produces a more heterogeneous MSRO pattern.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism should hold for fcc high‐entropy alloys where short-range order is measurable at the nanoscale and the alloying elements are known to interact strongly (e.g., Fe40Mn40Cr10Co10) under cryogenic deformation conditions.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in toughness and the optimal pre-annealing conditions remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples by applying different annealing treatments that yield (i) high CSRO and (ii) low CSRO levels. Deform both sets at 77 K under identical quasistatic strain-rate conditions. Conduct fracture toughness tests (e.g., three-point bending with pre-cracked specimens) and perform TEM/FFT mapping of the post-deformation MSRO distribution.
measurements: Fracture toughness parameters (e.g., KIC, Charpy energy absorption)
TEM/FFT imaging of MSRO morphology and connectivity
Quantitative analysis of initial CSRO via electron diffraction
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increased initial CSRO does not lead to a statistically significant enhancement in MSRO connectivity or a measurable improvement in fracture toughness relative to the low-CSRO baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C2

source_paper.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding in the paper that slow cooling coarsens γ′ precipitates to induce serrated boundaries, which are linked to reduced local strain concentration (PMC9848264::web::017).
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a modified cooling schedule—specifically an intermediate isothermal hold—to further control precipitate nucleation and coarsening dynamics at grain boundaries, thus refining the serration morphology for improved toughness retention, which was not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: An intermediate isothermal hold during cooling after solution treatment can optimize the nucleation and controlled coarsening of γ′ precipitates at grain boundaries, thereby enhancing the formation of uniform serrated boundaries that retain toughness at high temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: SLM‐fabricated high‐entropy alloy (Al8Co35Cr18Ni34Ti3Nb2Zr0.005B0.01) processed by a standard solution heat treatment at 1120°C with continuous slow cooling (as in HT‐2) that produces coarse γ′ precipitates and serrated grain boundaries.
hypothesis.intervention: After the 1120°C solution treatment, introduce an isothermal hold at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 1060°C) for a defined period (e.g., 30 minutes) prior to the final slow-cooling and subsequent aging at 750°C.
hypothesis.conditions: Samples are heated to 1120°C for 1 hour, then cooled to 1060°C where they are held isothermally for 30 minutes before continuing slow cooling (at 1°C/min) to 1000°C and finally air-cooling to room temperature prior to the aging heat treatment. Mechanical tests (tensile and creep) are performed at 650°C.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A uniform distribution of fine, initially nucleated γ′ precipitates at or near grain boundaries which then coarsen in a controlled manner to produce a consistent and well‐defined serrated morphology.
hypothesis.mechanism: The isothermal hold at 1060°C allows enhanced diffusion and nucleation of γ′ precipitates at the grain boundaries, creating multiple homogeneous nucleation sites. During subsequent cooling, these precipitates coarsen uniformly to induce a stable serrated boundary morphology. This structured serration is expected to distribute local strain more evenly, reducing strain concentration at triple junctions and thereby delaying intergranular crack propagation at 650°C (as shown in PMC9848264::web::017).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the standard continuous slow-cooling (HT-2) baseline, samples with an intermediate hold will exhibit improved high-temperature toughness as evidenced by higher tensile fracture strain and longer creep rupture life – potentially matching or exceeding the improvements observed (e.g., 3.5× or greater improvements in fracture strain).
hypothesis.baseline: HEA samples processed via standard HT-2 (solution treatment with continuous slow cooling) where serrated boundaries form but with a less uniform precipitate distribution.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected for HEAs operating at high temperatures (~650°C) where intergranular fracture due to localized stress concentrations predominates. Its effectiveness may depend on the alloy chemistry and diffusion rates; deviations in composition or thermal properties may alter the optimum hold temperature/time.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The ideal isothermal hold temperature and duration for optimum precipitate nucleation are not precisely known and may require calibration. The magnitude of toughness improvement is also subject to experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one group undergoing the intermediate isothermal hold and one control group with standard continuous slow-cooling (HT-2). Characterize the grain boundary morphology using SEM/EBSD and precipitate size/distribution via TEM, then perform tensile and creep tests at 650°C.
measurements: Grain boundary serration uniformity and precipitate distribution (via microscopy)
High-temperature tensile fracture strain
Creep rupture life and minimum creep strain rate
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intermediate hold samples do not show a statistically significant enhancement in grain boundary serration uniformity and corresponding improvements in high-temperature fracture strain and creep life relative to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C1

source_paper.title: Ductility Control via Nano-Precipitation at Grain Boundaries in Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta Multi-Principal Element Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: The evidence in the paper that grain boundary precipitates lead to ductility loss, combined with established concepts of grain boundary segregation improving cohesion as seen in superalloys.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a compositional modification (Boron addition) targeting grain boundary chemistry to decouple strengthening from embrittlement, a strategy not considered in the original study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Minor alloying with a grain boundary segregating element, such as Boron, can mitigate the adverse effects of precipitate-induced embrittlement by enhancing grain boundary cohesion, thereby promoting toughness retention even when some grain boundary precipitation occurs.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy composition similar to the Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta-Fe system that, under conventional aging conditions, develops grain boundary Hf2Fe precipitates causing a trade-off between strength and ductility.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a small addition (~0.1 atomic percent) of Boron during alloy synthesis.
hypothesis.conditions: Employ identical solution treatment and aging conditions (e.g., aging at 525°C for 30 minutes) for both the Boron-doped and undoped alloys.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at the grain boundaries, which alters the local chemistry and reduces the lattice mismatch stresses between the precipitates and matrix.
hypothesis.mechanism: Boron is known to segregate to grain boundaries (as seen in superalloys) and improve their cohesion. By stabilizing the grain boundaries, the negative impact of nano-precipitates acting as stress concentrators is reduced. This improved cohesion helps retain toughness even when precipitates are present to enhance strength.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The Boron-doped alloy should demonstrate a similar level of strength enhancement from precipitates but maintain or improve ductility (e.g., an increase in elongation by approximately 20–30% relative to the undoped counterpart) due to improved grain boundary integrity.
hypothesis.baseline: The performance of the undoped high-entropy alloy that exhibits a reduction in ductility (e.g., from 17.5% to around 7–14%) when grain boundary precipitates form.
hypothesis.boundary: This effect is expected in high-entropy alloys with similar compositions and grain sizes, under aging conditions that generate moderate precipitation levels, and when Boron is added in low concentrations so as not to form its own brittle phases.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in toughness is uncertain; quantitative effects will depend on the precise Boron content and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of high-entropy alloy samples – one with ~0.1 at.% Boron and one without. Process both sets identically (same solution treatment and aging at 525°C for 30 minutes). Characterize grain boundary chemistry using EDS and assess mechanical properties via tensile testing.
measurements: Grain boundary composition (Boron segregation level) via EDS.
Precipitate distribution (via SEM/TEM).
Mechanical properties: tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Boron-doped alloy does not show improved toughness (higher elongation at similar strength) compared to the undoped sample, or if new brittle phases form, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C3

source_paper.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s evidence that grain boundary decohesion due to nanoclustering leads to ductility loss, augmented by broader principles from grain boundary engineering.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis takes a novel approach by altering the intrinsic character of grain boundaries (enhancing Σ3 twin boundaries) through cyclic processing to physically suppress the embrittling nanosegregation mechanism, rather than relying solely on chemical changes or precipitate formation.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Tailoring the grain boundary character via processing to enhance the fraction of coherent Σ3 (twin) boundaries in CrMnFeCoNi HEA will reduce embrittling nanoclustering at GBs, thereby improving toughness at intermediate temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Single‐phase, coarse‐grained CrMnFeCoNi HEA produced by standard homogenization and annealing treatments (as in PMC6897545).
hypothesis.intervention: Implement a cyclic thermomechanical processing route – involving controlled cold deformation followed by a series of short, low-temperature annealing steps – optimized to induce deformation twins and increase the population of low-energy Σ3 twin boundaries.
hypothesis.conditions: Tensile tests performed at intermediate temperatures (400–800°C) under similar strain rate conditions. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) would be used to confirm the increased density of Σ3 twin boundaries.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A microstructure enriched in coherent Σ3 twin grain boundaries that are intrinsically low in energy and resistant to the rapid segregation of embrittling species.
hypothesis.mechanism: Coherent twin boundaries (Σ3 boundaries) generally exhibit lower interfacial energy and altered atomic structures relative to random high-angle grain boundaries, thereby reducing the driving force for segregation. This should impede the formation of brittle nanoclusters of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs, preserving ductility during testing at intermediate temperatures.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventionally processed HEA samples, the twin-boundary–enhanced alloy should display a reduced incidence of intergranular cracking and improved elongation under tensile conditions at intermediate temperatures. Although the degree of improvement may be moderate, measurable differences in toughness should be observed.
hypothesis.baseline: The standard recrystallized CrMnFeCoNi HEA with predominantly random high-angle grain boundaries that exhibit rapid ductility loss due to embrittling nanoclustering.
hypothesis.boundary: This hypothesis holds for high-entropy, single-phase fcc alloys where GB character can be effectively modified; it may be less effective if the processing does not yield a significant increase in Σ3 boundaries or if temperature-dependent diffusion overwhelms the GB character effect.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The extent to which enhancing Σ3 boundaries reduces embrittling segregation in this specific alloy is not fully quantified; the ideal processing parameters require optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA samples: one using conventional annealing (yielding mostly high-angle boundaries) and the other via cyclic deformation–annealing designed to maximize Σ3 twin boundaries. Validate the GB character using EBSD. Then, perform tensile tests at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 700°C).
measurements: EBSD to quantify the fraction of Σ3 boundaries
Tensile stress–strain curves to measure ductility and toughness
Microscopic analysis (APT/TEM-EDS) to assess the extent of embrittling element segregation at GBs.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples enriched in Σ3 twin boundaries do not show a statistically significant reduction in GB segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn and corresponding improvement in ductility compared with the baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi-Principal Element Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s findings that stable, nanoscale phase boundaries mediate dislocation transfer and crack bridging in dual‐phase HEAs.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis isolates the effect of interfacial spacing as a tunable parameter, proposing that controlled lamellar coarsening (not explored in the paper) will detrimentally affect toughness in a mechanistically explainable way.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Reducing phase boundary spacing enhances toughness retention in high‐entropy alloys by promoting continuous dislocation transfer and crack bridging; conversely, increasing the spacing will lead to premature loss of toughness.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A dual‐phase CoCrFeNiAl‐based HEA with an enamel‐like, nanolamellar structure (alternating FCC and BCC phases) as produced by additive manufacturing.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment to deliberately coarsen the lamellar microstructure, increasing the phase boundary spacing by approximately 20–30%.
hypothesis.conditions: Samples are tested under tensile loading up to high strains (similar to those in the baseline study) in ambient conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Nanolamellar phase boundaries between the FCC and BCC phases.
hypothesis.mechanism: Tighter phase boundaries mediate effective transfer of dislocations and promote crack deflection, bridging, and suppression of strain localization. Coarsening increases the spacing between these interfaces, reducing their ability to mediate stress transfer and energy dissipation, resulting in earlier strain localization and reduced toughness.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Heat‐treated samples with increased lamellar spacing should exhibit a lower static toughness and show earlier onset of strain localization and crack propagation compared with the as‐manufactured sample. The magnitude of the toughness drop is uncertain but expected to be statistically significant.
hypothesis.baseline: As‐manufactured AM samples with optimized nanoscale lamellar spacing as reported in the paper.
hypothesis.boundary: This hypothesis holds for HEAs with nanoscale dual‐phase structures where the interfacial spacing is critical; extreme grain coarsening or additional phase transformations would invalidate the mechanism.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative reduction in toughness is uncertain due to potential secondary diffusion or recovery effects during heat treatment.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) a control set of as‐manufactured HEA and (b) samples subjected to the controlled heat treatment to increase lamellar spacing. Perform in situ tensile tests with digital image correlation (DIC) to quantify strain localization and measure static toughness and strain‐hardening rates.
measurements: Tensile strength
Static toughness
Local strain distribution (DIC)
Crack path and bridging behavior (TEM/SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat‐treated samples do not show a statistically significant decrease in toughness or an earlier onset of strain localization compared to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C8

source_paper.title: Combining Machine Learning and Molecular Dynamics to Predict Mechanical Properties and Microstructural Evolution of FeNiCrCoCu High-Entropy Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s observation of a competing role between dislocation slip and twinning in governing mechanical asymmetry (PMC10058552::web::012, PMC10058552::web::016) and the known capability of nanoprecipitates to modify dislocation dynamics (TXT::wikipedia::Strengthening_mechanisms_of_materials::024)
hypotheses.what_is_new: This proposal specifically introduces an aging process to form engineered nanoprecipitates in the FeNiCrCoCu HEA—a processing route that modulates the classic competition between twin formation and dislocation slip to yield improved toughness retention, thereby extending the paper’s microstructural insights into a novel intervention.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Controlled nanoprecipitate formation via aging treatment improves toughness retention in FeNiCrCoCu HEA by modulating the competition between dislocation slip and twinning.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu HEA with the optimal composition (Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13) showing the intrinsic mixture of dislocation and twin activity under load as reported in the paper.
hypothesis.intervention: Execute a short-term aging treatment (post-solidification) at a temperature selected to induce fine, uniformly distributed nanoprecipitates without causing undesired phase transformations.
hypothesis.conditions: Perform mechanical tests (tensile and compressive) at room temperature and moderate temperatures under a consistent strain rate; the aging treatment parameters are to be optimized below the threshold for recrystallization.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The emergence of nanoscale precipitates that interact with mobile dislocations and twin boundaries, thereby distributing strain more uniformly.
hypothesis.mechanism: The nanoprecipitates serve as obstacles to both dislocation motion and twin boundary migration. This pinning effect forces dislocations to bow and accumulate over a broader area, leading to a more distributed plastic deformation. Consequently, localized stress concentrations are less severe, delaying crack initiation and propagation, and resulting in enhanced toughness retention. This mechanism is distinct because it capitalizes on a controlled microstructural modification—nanoprecipitate formation—to alter the inherent deformation dynamics of the HEA.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy (without aging-induced precipitates), the aged HEA should demonstrate a smoother stress–strain response with a smaller sudden drop in stress beyond peak load, increased ductility, and higher fracture toughness. There is also an expectation of increased uniformity in the microstructural evolution during deformation.
hypothesis.baseline: Fe33Ni32Cr11Co11Cu13 HEA produced without any additional aging treatment designed to promote nanoprecipitate formation.
hypothesis.boundary: The hypothesis should hold within a pre-defined aging temperature window and aging time regime where nanoprecipitates form optimally; aging outside this window may lead to coarsening or unwanted phases, invalidating the expected behavior.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise size, volume fraction, and spatial distribution of precipitates necessary for optimal toughening effect are uncertain until calibrated experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one as baseline without additional aging and one subjected to the controlled aging treatment to induce nanoprecipitation. Characterize the microstructure via TEM to confirm nanoprecipitate formation and conduct fracture toughness tests as well as detailed stress–strain measurements.
measurements: Fracture toughness (K_IC)
Stress–strain behavior (noting the nature of stress drop post-yield)
Nanoprecipitate size, volume fraction, and distribution (via TEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a significant improvement in toughness (as evidenced by less abrupt stress drop and higher K_IC) along with confirmed nanoprecipitate formation relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C9

source_paper.title: Probing the microstructure and deformation mechanism of an FeCoCrNiAl0.5 high entropy alloy during nanoscratching: a combined atomistic and physical model study.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding or mechanism of the paper this hypothesis starts from
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a post-deformation, dynamic recovery route tailored specifically for HEAs to optimize dislocation network characteristics and delay strain localization, a mechanism distinct from the direct dislocation strengthening evaluated in the original nanoscratching simulations.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A controlled post-cold-work, subcritical annealing (dynamic recovery) treatment can tailor the dislocation structure in FeCoCrNiAl0.5 HEA to an optimal intermediate density that delays strain localization and enhances toughness retention.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A cold-worked FeCoCrNiAl0.5 HEA that, as observed in the MD simulations, exhibits rapidly evolving dislocation densities and stacking fault formation leading to localized deformation.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject the cold-worked HEA to a carefully controlled subcritical annealing treatment (at temperatures below the recrystallization threshold) to promote dynamic recovery by facilitating limited dislocation annihilation and rearrangement without significant grain growth.
hypothesis.conditions: Annealing temperature and duration must be optimized to partially relieve dislocation tangling while retaining a high level of lattice distortion and avoiding full recrystallization. Mechanical testing should be performed at room temperature under both quasi-static and dynamic loading conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: An optimally recovered dislocation network that balances stored dislocation density and homogeneous stress distribution, thereby minimizing localized strain bursts and crack initiation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Cold working induces a high density of dislocations which can lead to strain localization and premature failure. A subcritical annealing treatment promotes dynamic recovery—a process where excess dislocations are annihilated or rearranged into lower-energy configurations—thus reducing stress concentrations while preserving beneficial lattice distortion. This moderated dislocation density is hypothesized to improve the distribution of plastic deformation and delay the onset of strain localization, enhancing toughness retention.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to both the as-cold-worked and as-solutionized states, the dynamically recovered HEA is expected to exhibit improved fracture toughness and ductility (with a more uniform strain distribution), although the yield strength may be slightly reduced. The improvement should be detectable via standard fracture and fatigue tests.
hypothesis.baseline: The cold-worked HEA with high dislocation densities and localized stacking faults as produced in the MD simulations, and the as-solutionized material with lower pre-existing dislocation density.
hypothesis.boundary: This approach benefits toughness when the annealing is conducted under conditions that promote dynamic recovery without triggering recrystallization; if the temperature or time is too high, grain coarsening or loss of intrinsic lattice distortion may occur, negating the toughness benefit.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise processing window (temperature–time parameters) for achieving the optimal balance between dislocation density and recovery is not precisely predictable without experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare FeCoCrNiAl0.5 HEA specimens that have been cold worked to a significant strain. Subject subsets of these to various subcritical annealing regimes (varying temperature and duration). Characterize dislocation structures using TEM and measure fracture toughness (using bending or impact tests) to determine the relationship between dislocation density and toughness.
measurements: Dislocation density and network characterization (TEM, X-ray line broadening)
Fracture toughness and ductility (standard fracture tests, bending tests)
Grain size verification (EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples treated under any subcritical annealing conditions do not show improved toughness (or if toughness decreases relative to the as-cold-worked condition due to over-recovery), then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: Rejuvenation as the origin of planar defects in the CrCoNi medium entropy alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the finding that dislocation glide destroys SRO and reduces SF energy in the CrCoNi MEA (PMC10873362::web::017::discussion)
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a pre-mechanical-test thermal treatment to deliberately tailor the SRO state, connecting initial SRO levels to subsequent rejuvenation dynamics and toughness, which was not addressed in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Altering the thermal processing to control the degree of short-range order (SRO) in HEAs will modulate the rejuvenation-induced planar defect evolution, thereby governing toughness retention. Specifically, increasing the initial SRO (via slower cooling or annealing) will lead to a higher initial stacking fault (SF) energy and reduced inelastic rejuvenation during cyclic loading, resulting in less crack-tip blunting and lower toughness retention compared to a rapidly quenched state.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An equiatomic high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrCoNi based) processed by rapid quenching to preserve a moderate level of SRO.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce a controlled thermal annealing treatment prior to mechanical testing to increase the degree of SRO (or a slower cooling process) and thus raise the initial SF energy.
hypothesis.conditions: Subject both the annealed (high-SRO) and the rapidly-quenched (lower-SRO) samples to identical cyclic loading tests at room temperature under in situ electron microscopy.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The degree of SRO that sets the SF energy and the subsequent dissociation behavior of dislocations.
hypothesis.mechanism: A higher pre-existing SRO results in a larger driving force for restoring order (higher SF energy) after dislocation glide. Consequently, the reversible formation of SFs dominates and rejuvenation is minimized. This reduced planar defect evolution at the crack tip leads to less effective crack blunting, thereby affecting toughness retention. In contrast, a lower initial SRO permits easier dislocation-induced disruption and irreversible SF formation (rejuvenation), enhancing ductile blunting.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The annealed, higher-SRO alloy will show less increase in irreversible SF length and a smaller degree of crack-tip plasticity (blunting) over many cycles; hence, it will exhibit lower toughness retention compared to the quenched alloy. The magnitude of the effect is expected to be significant qualitatively, though precise quantitative predictions are uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: The original quenched CrCoNi MEA with moderate SRO showing a two-phase evolution of SFs and enhanced crack-tip blunting after cyclic loading (as reported in PMC10873362).
hypothesis.boundary: The hypothesis should hold for HEAs with FCC structure under cyclic loading at room temperature. Extreme thermal treatments that induce phase transformations or grain coarsening are outside the boundary.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by observation of SRO-related SF energy changes in the paper, the precise quantitative relationship between SRO fraction and toughness retention in different thermal states remains to be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrCoNi MEA samples: one rapidly quenched and one undergoing a controlled annealing cycle to enhance SRO. Subject both sets to identical cyclic loading protocols while using in situ 4D-STEM to monitor SF length evolution and crack-tip morphology.
measurements: SF average length
density and reversibility of SFs
crack-tip opening displacement (CTOD)
fracture toughness tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in irreversible SF evolution and less crack blunting relative to the quenched samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C11

source_paper.title: Rejuvenation as the origin of planar defects in the CrCoNi medium entropy alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observation that SRO governs SF energy and defect reversibility in HEAs (PMC10873362::web::017::discussion)
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a compositional modification by minor alloying to actively stabilize SRO, thereby directly linking chemical ordering to the resistance against rejuvenation under cyclic loading—a strategy not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporating minor alloying elements that promote stronger atomic ordering (i.e., stabilize SRO) will inhibit the dislocation-induced rejuvenation in HEAs, thereby reducing the irreversible evolution of planar defects and leading to lower toughness retention under cyclic loading.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An equiatomic HEA (such as CrCoNi) with a known degree of SRO and exhibiting reversible-to-irreversible SF transitions under cyclic loading.
hypothesis.intervention: Doping the alloy with a small quantity (few atomic percent) of a stabilizer element (e.g., a refractory metal or element known to enhance local chemical ordering) during casting.
hypothesis.conditions: Conduct cyclic loading tests under identical conditions (room temperature, same loading amplitude and frequency) for both the doped and undoped alloys, with in situ characterization of defect evolution.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Local atomic ordering (SRO) that influences the SF formation energy and the associated reversible or irreversible defect structures.
hypothesis.mechanism: The dopant increases the binding energy among specific atomic pairs, leading to a more robust SRO that resists dislocation-induced breakdown. This limits the reduction in SF energy during cyclic loading, keeping SFs predominantly reversible and thus diminishing the formation of long, irreversible SFs and twins that are instrumental in crack-tip blunting. As a result, the doped alloy would show lower ductility-enhanced toughness (i.e., reduced ability to blunt cracks) compared with the undoped counterpart.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The doped alloy should exhibit a lower increase in SF length and less pronounced crack-tip blunting after many loading cycles, leading to reduced toughness retention (i.e., less damage tolerance improvement) relative to the undoped alloy. The direction is clear, but the magnitude of change is moderately uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: Undoped CrCoNi MEA as detailed in PMC10873362, which shows significant rejuvenation with increasing SF length and improved crack-tip blunting after cyclic loading.
hypothesis.boundary: The hypothesis applies to HEAs with FCC structures under cyclic loading conditions at room temperature; effects due to large dopant levels or secondary phase precipitation are excluded.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the dopant-induced stabilization of SRO is a known concept, the quantitative influence on SF energy and the resulting toughness retention might vary, and the optimal dopant concentration is not precisely predicted.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two HEA samples: an undoped CrCoNi MEA and a doped variant with a small concentration of the selected stabilizing element. Apply identical cyclic loading regimes and perform in situ 4D-STEM to track SF evolution and crack-tip morphology. Additionally, carry out standardized fracture toughness measurements.
measurements: SF length distribution
frequency of irreversible SFs
CTOD
fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the doped alloy exhibits a similar or greater degree of SF rejuvenation (irreversible defect formation and crack-tip blunting) and no significant drop in toughness retention compared to the undoped alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: Investigation of the Micromechanical Behavior of a Ti68Nb7Ta3Zr4Mo18 (at.%) High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the observation in PMC10383748 that finer grains in the HEA do not yield expected strengthening due to grain boundary instability and dislocation behavior.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a controlled processing route (thermomechanical grain size modification) specifically aimed at balancing dislocation and grain boundary contributions to toughness retention, rather than solely focusing on strength or phase transformation.

expert_context.question: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges?
