Fracture surface morphology (SEM)
Engineering stress-strain response (tensile testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no statistically significant difference in the extent of GB nanoclustering or fracture mode is observed between low and high strain rates, then the hypothesis that strain rate modulates dislocation-enhanced nanoclustering is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C12

source_paper.title: Influence of Degree of Severe Plastic Deformation on Thermal Stability of an HfNbTiZr Multi-Principal Element Alloy Processed by High-Pressure Torsion.

hypotheses.builds_on: The observed bcc phase splitting into bccL and bccH (PMC9565433::web::018) combined with established principles of grain-boundary segregation (TXT::wikipedia::Segregation_(materials_science)::002).
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically links the degree of deformation (shear strain) to enhanced grain-boundary segregation of a particular phase (bccL) in HEAs and correlates this local chemical inhomogeneity directly with a transition toward brittle (intergranular) fracture—a mechanistic pathway not examined in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Enhanced grain‐boundary segregation of the Hf/Zr‐rich bccL phase in high-strain HEA regions promotes interfacial decohesion and brittle fracture.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase HfNbTiZr high-entropy alloy processed by HPT, with a homogeneous bcc structure and a uniform distribution of the four elements.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject separate batches of the HEA to different degrees of shear strain using HPT (e.g., selecting regions near the disk center for low strain and near the edge for high strain). Anneal all samples between 740 K and 890 K under identical conditions to induce bcc phase splitting. Use atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM coupled with EDS mapping specifically at and near grain boundaries to quantify the segregation of the Hf/Zr-enriched bccL phase.
hypothesis.conditions: Room-temperature mechanical fracture tests (micro-cantilever bending or notched specimens) performed at a fixed loading rate; annealing times and quenching rates kept constant to isolate the effects of strain-induced diffusion and segregation.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that become enriched in bccL phase owing to accelerated diffusion along high-angle boundaries in regions of high imposed strain.
hypothesis.mechanism: High shear strain increases the density of defects and grain-boundary area, which in turn accelerates grain-boundary diffusion during subsequent annealing. As the single-phase bcc matrix decomposes into bccL (enriched in larger Hf/Zr atoms) and bccH phases, the bccL phase preferentially diffuses and segregates to grain boundaries where diffusion pathways are more active. This localized enrichment reduces the interfacial cohesion (due to the lower bonding strength associated with the larger atomic radii), therefore predisposing these boundaries to intergranular brittle fracture under load.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: High-strain specimens will exhibit a measurable increase (qualitatively observed by APT/TEM-EDS) of Hf/Zr concentration at grain boundaries relative to low-strain specimens. Corresponding fracture tests will show lower fracture toughness and predominantly intergranular fracture modes in high-strain samples compared to the ductile behavior of specimens without significant grain-boundary enrichment.
hypothesis.baseline: The as-HPT processed HEA showing a homogeneous single-phase bcc structure with no preferential grain-boundary segregation and high toughness under comparable fracture tests.
hypothesis.boundary: Applies to HEA service conditions where the material is thermally exposed in the range of 740–890 K, without forming extensive intermetallic precipitates, and where deformation-induced strain heterogeneity exists.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact quantitative threshold of segregated Hf/Zr at the grain boundaries necessary for a significant drop in interfacial cohesion is not fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Process HEA specimens via HPT to create low- and high-strain regions, anneal at 740–890 K for a fixed time, and quench rapidly. Conduct APT and high-resolution TEM/EDS mapping focused on grain boundaries to compare local chemical composition. Perform fracture toughness tests (e.g., micro-cantilever bending) and fractographic analyses to relate grain-boundary composition with fracture mode.
measurements: Grain-boundary chemical profiles (Hf/Zr concentrations) from APT/TEM-EDS
Fracture toughness values
Fracture surface morphology (intergranular vs. transgranular features)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high-strain samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in Hf/Zr segregation at grain boundaries compared to low-strain samples or if their fracture toughness is comparable with a predominance of transgranular fracture, then the hypothesis is refuted.

hypotheses.label: C8

source_paper.title: Exceptional damage-tolerance of a medium-entropy alloy CrCoNi at cryogenic temperatures.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation that earlier onset of deformation nano-twinning is key to exceptional damage tolerance.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis links the effect of grain size on the activation of nano-twinning to toughness degradation in high-entropy alloys, providing a new avenue distinct from traditional segregation-induced embrittlement.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Grain Size–Mediated Suppression of Nano-Twinning and Toughness Degradation
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A recrystallized, single-phase high-entropy alloy exhibiting a fine equiaxed grain structure with abundant deformation-induced nano-twins.
hypothesis.intervention: Tailor the microstructure via controlled annealing to produce samples with significantly coarser grain sizes while preserving phase stability and overall composition.
hypothesis.conditions: Samples with fine grain sizes (e.g., 5–10 μm) versus coarse grain sizes (e.g., >40 μm) tested under the same cryogenic and ambient temperature mechanical loading conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Grain size and the associated density of twin nucleation sites.
hypothesis.mechanism: The paper shows that nano-twinning enhances damage tolerance by contributing to strain hardening and delaying plastic instability. Coarser grains are less effective at nucleating and propagating deformation nano-twins. As a result, the strain-hardening capacity is reduced, and localized plastic strains accumulate at grain boundaries, leading to brittle fracture. This contrasts with conventional alloys where embrittlement is often due to grain-boundary segregation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Coarse-grained samples will exhibit lower ductility, reduced work hardening (lower strain-hardening exponent), and lower fracture toughness compared to fine-grained counterparts. Fracture surfaces are expected to show less evidence of twin-mediated plasticity and more cleavage-like features.
hypothesis.baseline: The baseline is the high ductility and high toughness behavior observed in the fine-grained single-phase alloy in the reference study (PMC4740901).
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is most critical under loading conditions where nano-twinning is the dominant source of plasticity, typically at cryogenic and room temperatures.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise threshold grain size at which twin suppression becomes dominant is uncertain and may vary with alloy chemistry.

falsification_experiment.design: Process high-entropy alloy samples to obtain two distinct grain size distributions. Conduct tensile and fracture tests at identical temperatures and strain rates, followed by microstructural characterization (EBSD) to quantify nano-twin density.
measurements: Grain size (via EBSD)
Strain-hardening exponent
Fracture toughness (KJIc, JIc values)
Density of deformation twins
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If coarse-grained samples do not exhibit a significant reduction in deformation nano-twinning and concurrently maintain comparable toughness and ductility to fine-grained samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C4

source_paper.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s observation that minimal trace elements (C and B) in standard HEAs are insufficient to prevent nano‐segregation-induced GB embrittlement.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis intentionally increases boron content to modify GB chemistry, leveraging microalloying strategies familiar in conventional alloys but applying them to counteract nanoclustering in compositionally complex HEAs.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Enhancing grain boundary cohesion in single-phase HEAs by deliberate microalloying with elevated boron levels can counteract embrittlement. The hypothesis posits that sufficient boron segregation to grain boundaries will competitively inhibit the nanoclustering of embrittling Cr, Ni, and Mn, thereby mitigating intergranular cracking at intermediate temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A standard, single-phase CrMnFeCoNi HEA with nominally trace amounts of B (≈0.008 at %), which exhibits ductility loss via GB nanoclustering at intermediate temperatures.
hypothesis.intervention: Increase the boron content (e.g., to 0.2–0.5 at %) during alloy preparation while maintaining overall compositional complexity and single-phase stability.
hypothesis.conditions: Tensile testing at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 700°C) under identical deformation and environmental conditions for both B-enhanced and standard HEA samples.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at grain boundaries altering the local chemistry and energy landscape.
hypothesis.mechanism: At elevated concentrations, boron has a strong affinity for grain boundaries, where it can lower the GB energy and occupy sites that would otherwise accommodate nanoclusters of Cr, Ni, and Mn. This competitive segregation limits the formation of deleterious nanoclusters, preserves GB cohesion, and delays brittle fracture initiation compared to conventional HEAs. Unlike conventional alloys where impurity segregation is often inadvertent and deleterious, here boron is purposefully added to stabilize the GB structure.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The B-enhanced alloy will show a reduced extent of nanoclustering of the principal embrittling elements at GBs (detectable via APT/TEM), exhibit a more ductile (transgranular) fracture mode, and demonstrate improved toughness at 700°C relative to the standard alloy.
hypothesis.baseline: The standard CrMnFeCoNi HEA with minimal boron, which shows pronounced GB nanoclustering and brittle intergranular failure at intermediate temperatures.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected if boron does not precipitate as brittle borides; thus, the upper limit of B addition must be below the threshold for secondary phase formation. The improvement is relevant primarily at intermediate to high temperatures where diffusion allows segregation.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal boron concentration is uncertain; too high a level may lead to the formation of brittle compounds, complicating interpretation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA samples: one with standard boron content and another with elevated boron (within the solubility limits that maintain single-phase structure). Perform tensile tests at 700°C and analyze GB composition (APT/EDS) and fracture surfaces (SEM).
measurements: Grain boundary boron concentration (APT/EDS)
Extent of Cr, Ni, Mn nanoclustering (APT/TEM)
Fracture mode and tensile ductility (mechanical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the elevated-B alloy does not show significantly reduced embrittling element nanoclustering at GBs or improved ductility compared to the standard alloy, then the hypothesis that boron competitively inhibits deleterious segregation is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C5

source_paper.title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the established concept in conventional alloys that selective environmental interactions at grain boundaries (e.g., oxidation) lead to embrittlement, extended here into the HEA regime where complexity may initially suppress such effects (TXT::wikipedia::Intermetallic::003)
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis explores the specific role of controlled oxygen exposure in degrading grain-boundary cohesion in a compositionally complex HEA—a mechanism that contrasts with the usual emphasis on elemental segregation in conventional alloys.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Exposure of a single-phase HEA to a moderately oxidizing environment at elevated temperatures leads to preferential grain-boundary oxidation, which degrades intergranular cohesion and triggers brittle fracture even though the bulk remains compositionally complex.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, single-phase HEA with a fine, uniform BCC solid-solution matrix and chemically even grain boundaries.
hypothesis.intervention: Age the HEA in a controlled atmosphere that contains a low partial pressure of oxygen (e.g., 10^-4 atm) at elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C) for a defined period, and compare with samples aged under an inert atmosphere.
hypothesis.conditions: Aging experiments conducted in two environments (oxidizing vs inert) under identical thermal profiles; mechanical testing performed post-aging at room temperature.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Formation of thin, oxygen-rich oxide layers selectively along grain boundaries that become chemically distinct and mechanically weaker than the bulk matrix.
hypothesis.mechanism: Even in a compositionally stable HEA, the grain boundaries may serve as fast diffusion pathways for oxygen. Under moderate oxidizing conditions at elevated temperatures, oxygen preferentially accumulates at these boundaries to form a brittle oxide phase. This oxide layer reduces grain-boundary cohesion, thereby predisposing the alloy to intergranular brittle fracture upon mechanical loading. The mechanism mimics conventional oxidation-assisted embrittlement but is applied here to a compositionally complex HEA.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: HEA samples aged in an oxidizing environment will show measurable oxide layers at grain boundaries (via XPS or TEM analysis) and, upon mechanical testing, a shift toward intergranular fracture with reduced toughness compared to samples aged in an inert atmosphere.
hypothesis.baseline: As-processed, single-phase HEA with robust grain-boundary cohesion and ductile, transgranular fracture modes.
hypothesis.boundary: Applicable to service conditions where HEAs are exposed to moderate oxygen levels at elevated temperatures; relevance may be limited in fully protective environments.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The rate of oxidation and the thickness of the oxide layer depend on oxygen activity and may be subtle; the exact impact on toughness might vary with slight changes in environmental parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical HEA specimens and age one set in an oxygen-containing atmosphere (controlled partial pressure) and another set in an inert atmosphere under otherwise identical thermal conditions. After aging, perform detailed chemical analyses (TEM, XPS, or APT) at the grain boundaries and conduct mechanical tests (tensile/compression) to assess toughness and fracture mode.
measurements: Grain-boundary oxide layer detection by high-resolution TEM and XPS
Mechanical toughness (load-displacement curves) and fracture mode analysis via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens aged in the oxidizing atmosphere do not reveal distinct grain-boundary oxide layers and their mechanical properties (fracture toughness and mode) are similar to those aged in an inert atmosphere, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C6

source_paper.title: Effects of Annealing on Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Metastable Powder Metallurgy CoCrFeNiMo0.2 High Entropy Alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: The paper’s established link between heat-treatment-induced precipitation and mechanical performance, combined with concepts from grain-boundary engineering that highlight the impact of spatially inhomogeneous microstructures on toughening.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This approach separates the kinetic pathways for intra- and intergranular precipitation by using a tailored two-stage heat treatment, providing a new means to test whether localized grain-boundary coarsening is the primary driver of brittle behavior in a HEA.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Brittle behavior emerges in the HEA due to a mismatch in precipitation kinetics between grain interiors and grain boundaries, resulting in an uneven distribution of reinforcing precipitates that causes localized embrittlement at boundaries.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A fully recrystallized, metastable single-phase CoCrFeNiMo0.2 HEA with a homogeneous grain structure.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement a two-stage heat-treatment process: first, a high-temperature step to nucleate fine intragranular precipitates, followed by a lower-temperature aging step to limit further grain-boundary precipitation.
hypothesis.conditions: Apply the two-stage treatment under controlled atmospheres (vacuum or inert gas) and compare with a conventional single-stage high-temperature anneal that promotes both intra- and intergranular precipitation.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The spatial distribution and size difference of the σ-phase precipitates between the grain interiors and the grain boundaries.
hypothesis.mechanism: The high-temperature step uniformly nucleates nanoscale precipitates within the grains, while the subsequent low-temperature aging minimizes diffusion along grain boundaries, thereby suppressing excessive intergranular precipitation. If brittle behavior is primarily due to the formation of coarse, contiguous precipitates at grain boundaries, then the two-stage treatment should yield a tougher alloy by improving the homogeneity of the microstructure. This stands apart from conventional alloys where grain-boundary segregation alone is implicated; here, differential kinetics in a HEA setting play a predominant role.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The two-stage heat treatment should result in a more uniform dispersion of fine precipitates, reduced intergranular precipitation, and improved toughness relative to the single-stage annealed sample, which is expected to exhibit more grain-boundary coarsening and brittle intergranular failure. Improvements in ductility and delayed crack propagation are anticipated.
hypothesis.baseline: The single-stage heat-treated CoCrFeNiMo0.2 HEA that exhibits both intra- and intergranular precipitation as described in the paper.
hypothesis.boundary: Ambient temperature deformation under tension; the mechanism is relevant in service conditions where uniform mechanical performance is critical.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The optimal temperatures and durations for both stages to achieve the desired differential precipitation suppression are not fully determined beforehand.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of HEA samples: one processed via the two-stage heat-treatment and one via the conventional single-stage annealing. Characterize the spatial distribution of precipitates (using TEM and EBSD) and perform tensile and fracture toughness tests.
measurements: Precipitate size and location distribution (intragranular vs. intergranular)
Tensile mechanical properties (yield strength, elongation, toughness)
Fractographic analysis to determine the crack initiation sites
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the two-stage heat-treated samples do not show a significant reduction in grain-boundary precipitate coarsening and do not exhibit improved ductility and toughness compared to the single-stage samples, or if failure still predominates along grain boundaries, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C7

source_paper.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the traditional understanding that even subtle segregation at grain boundaries can impair toughness, combined with the insight that in conventional HEAs slow cooling typically leads to beneficial precipitate-induced serration—this hypothesis tests the mechanism in a system engineered to avoid precipitate formation.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a new pathway for embrittlement in HEAs by isolating and examining the effect of elemental segregation on grain boundaries in the absence of precipitate formation, a scenario not addressed in the original paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: In HEAs with Suppressed γ′ Precipitation, Slow Cooling Induces Detrimental Elemental Grain Boundary Segregation
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An initially single‐phase, compositionally complex HEA fabricated by SLM modified in composition to suppress γ′ precipitation (e.g., by reducing Ti and/or Al content) so that the alloy remains single-phase upon slow cooling.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement two post-solution cooling protocols on the modified composition: (a) rapid water quenching and (b) slow cooling at 1°C/min, ensuring that precipitate formation is minimized so that any differences in toughness arise from elemental redistribution rather than precipitate-induced serrated boundaries.
hypothesis.conditions: After solution treatment above the (suppressed) solvus temperature, process one set by rapid quench and the other by controlled slow cooling (1°C/min) to room temperature; then perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests at 650°C.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Subtle elemental segregation at grain boundaries (detected by atom probe tomography or high-resolution EDS) altering local bonding and reducing grain-boundary cohesion without the formation of second-phase precipitates.
hypothesis.mechanism: In the absence of beneficial coarse precipitates that normally pin and serrate boundaries, slow cooling allows certain solute elements (such as Nb, Zr, or B) to segregate to grain boundaries. This segregation can lower the cohesive strength of the boundaries and promote brittle intergranular fracture under high-temperature loading.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: For the modified HEA, the slow-cooled specimens should exhibit lower tensile fracture strain and shorter creep rupture life at 650°C compared to rapidly quenched specimens, due to degraded grain boundary cohesion. The magnitude of embrittlement is expected to be moderate, though exact values are uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: Rapidly quenched specimens of the modified HEA, showing minimal grain-boundary segregation and hence relatively higher toughness at elevated temperatures.
hypothesis.boundary: The effect is most pronounced under high-temperature (650°C) conditions where weakened grain boundaries are stressed; at room temperature, the mechanical differences might be less evident.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The extent of deleterious segregation and its quantitative impact on toughness in the absence of precipitate formation remains to be fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the compositionally modified HEA (with suppressed γ′ formation) using identical solution treatments but differing only in cooling rate (rapid quench vs. slow cooling). Analyze grain boundary chemistry using atom probe tomography or high-resolution EDS, then perform high-temperature tensile and creep tests at 650°C.
measurements: Grain boundary elemental composition
Tensile fracture strain at 650°C
Creep rupture life at 650°C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both cooling protocols yield similar grain boundary compositions and the slow-cooled specimens do not exhibit reduced toughness compared to the quenched specimens, then the hypothesis that slow cooling induces harmful segregation is refuted.

hypotheses.label: C2

source_paper.title: Deformation-induced grain boundary segregation in a powder-metallurgy ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy.

hypotheses.builds_on: the paper’s findings on deformation-induced segregation and the general importance of grain boundary chemistry in determining mechanical cohesion
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes that it is the heterogeneity in grain boundary segregation—not merely the presence of segregation—that drives residual stress concentrations leading to brittle failure, offering a novel perspective on toughness degradation in HEAs.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Heterogeneous Grain Boundary Segregation Generates Residual Stress Concentrations that Promote Brittle Fracture.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A single-phase HEA with uniform elemental distribution and a largely homogeneous microstructure prior to deformation.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement a deformation process that applies a spatial gradient in strain (for example, via controlled bending or gradient compression tests) to induce non-uniform segregation. Compare regions experiencing high strain gradients (and thus higher segregation heterogeneity) with regions of more uniform deformation.
hypothesis.conditions: Use deformation techniques that inherently produce spatial variations in strain–rate across the sample. After processing, perform localized mechanical testing and residual stress measurements at room or elevated temperatures relevant to service conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries with heterogeneous segregation profiles, where local accumulation of refractory elements creates internal residual tensile stresses.
hypothesis.mechanism: Non-uniform segregation at grain boundaries can result in localized compositional variations, which alter the lattice parameter and induce residual stress fields within the intergranular regions. These residual tensile stresses add to applied loads, thereby reducing the effective cohesive strength of the boundaries and facilitating the initiation and propagation of intergranular cracks under mechanical stress.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Regions exhibiting high segregation heterogeneity will display higher residual tensile stresses (detectable via high-resolution X-ray diffraction or synchrotron methods) and lower fracture toughness, with fracture surfaces showing intergranular characteristics. Uniformly deformed regions should maintain lower residual stresses and preserve ductility.
hypothesis.baseline: Regions of the HEA that experience uniform deformation, resulting in homogeneous grain boundaries, low residual stress levels, and ductile fracture behavior.
hypothesis.boundary: The effect is most important in service conditions where strain gradients (e.g., bending or non-uniform loading) produce significant segregation heterogeneity. Under uniformly applied loads, this mechanism may be diminished.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Quantitative linkage between specific residual stress levels caused by segregation heterogeneity and fracture toughness reduction requires further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate HEA samples by applying a deformation process that produces a controlled gradient in strain. Map the residual stress distribution using synchrotron XRD or high-resolution XRD and assess local segregation with atom probe tomography or TEM-EDS. Conduct localized fracture toughness tests (e.g., micro-cantilever bending) in regions with different segregation levels. Correlate the magnitudes of residual stress with local toughness measurements.
measurements: Residual stress maps via high-resolution XRD
Local chemical segregation profiles (APT or TEM-EDS)
Localized fracture toughness data
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If regions with high segregation heterogeneity do not exhibit elevated residual tensile stresses or if the local fracture toughness is not significantly reduced compared to uniformly deformed regions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C11

source_paper.title: Microstructure and Room Temperature Mechanical Properties of Different 3 and 4 Element Medium Entropy Alloys from HfNbTaTiZr System.

hypotheses.builds_on: The observed correlation between Ta/Zr segregation and loss of ductility in the paper, combined with established superalloy practice that boron improves grain-boundary cohesion.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces a minor alloying element (boron) as a microstructural modifier aimed at mitigating segregation-induced embrittlement in a complex HEA while retaining its compositional complexity.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor amount of a grain-boundary cohesion enhancer (such as boron) into a compositionally complex HEA suppresses the detrimental effects of Ta and Zr segregation, thereby retaining toughness even if local segregation tendencies exist.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An initially homogeneous HfNbTaTiZr HEA with known sensitivity to Ta and Zr segregation.
hypothesis.intervention: Minor alloying addition of approximately 0.5 atomic percent boron during the melting process.
hypothesis.conditions: Casting under identical conditions with rapid cooling to preserve the single-phase state; subsequent room temperature tensile testing; comparative analysis between boron-doped and undoped alloys.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Boron atoms segregate to grain boundaries, increasing boundary cohesion and potentially interacting with segregating Ta and Zr to inhibit detrimental precipitate nucleation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Boron has been used in other alloy systems (e.g., superalloys) to improve grain-boundary cohesion and reduce embrittlement. By preferentially segregating to grain boundaries, boron may lower the energy of these interfaces and diminish the driving force for Ta/Zr precipitation as indicated by known segregation principles (TXT::wikipedia::Segregation_(materials_science)::002). This stabilizes the microstructure and maintains a higher fraction of the ductile BCC1 phase.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The boron-doped HEA is expected to exhibit higher elongation to failure and a more ductile fracture morphology than the undoped baseline. Improvements in toughness are anticipated to be significant relative to the brittle behavior observed in Ta+Zr enriched compositions.
hypothesis.baseline: A rapidly quenched, undoped HfNbTaTiZr HEA that under identical conditions shows some level of grain-boundary segregation leading to reduced ductility.
hypothesis.boundary: Effectiveness may be limited to room temperature tensile behavior; the influence may differ under high-temperature service due to altered diffusion kinetics.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of toughness improvement is uncertain due to potential interactions of boron with other elements and the complexity of grain-boundary chemistry.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfNbTaTiZr HEA samples, one with 0.5 at% boron and one without. Subject both to identical casting and rapid quench procedures. Perform room temperature tensile tests and microstructural analyses (SEM and grain boundary composition via WDS) to compare ductility and grain-boundary morphology.
measurements: Tensile elongation to failure
Fracture toughness
Grain-boundary element mapping (focus on boron, Ta, Zr)
Phase analysis of BCC content
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of boron does not lead to a statistically significant improvement in ductility or if no enhanced grain-boundary cohesion (i.e., reduction in brittle precipitates) is observed relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C1

source_paper.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi-Principal Element Alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: the mechanism of phase-boundary mediated dislocation transfer described in the paper.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It tests the temperature sensitivity of the phase-boundary mediated toughening mechanism in HEAs, providing a controlled comparison to conventional alloy behavior under low-temperature conditions.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Brittle behavior emerges in the HEA at low temperatures due to suppressed dislocation nucleation and impaired phase-boundary mediated plasticity.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: An initially single-phase, compositionally complex HEA with alternating FCC and BCC lamellae that facilitates continuous dislocation migration as demonstrated in the paper.
hypothesis.intervention: Perform controlled tensile tests at cryogenic (e.g., -100 °C) versus room temperature and adjust the strain rate to investigate temperature-dependent dislocation activity.
hypothesis.conditions: Low testing temperatures and moderate strain rates where thermal activation for dislocation nucleation is limited.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: The nanoscale phase boundaries between FCC and BCC phases which normally mediate dislocation transfer.
hypothesis.mechanism: At cryogenic temperatures, the energy barrier for dislocation nucleation and migration increases significantly. As a result, the phase-boundary mediated mechanism that relies on continuous dislocation transfer becomes inefficient. This leads to early strain localization, minimal plastic deformation, and preferential brittle crack propagation along or near the phase boundaries, in contrast to the ductile behavior at higher temperatures.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Under cryogenic testing, the HEA will exhibit a lower uniform elongation, a sharper decline in strain-hardening rate, and fracture surfaces with more cleavage features compared to the ductile baseline at room temperature.
hypothesis.baseline: The conventional performance of the HEA at room temperature, featuring strong work-hardening and energy dissipation via active dislocation transfer.
hypothesis.boundary: Valid for service conditions where the operating temperature drops near or below cryogenic levels; at intermediate temperatures, the effect may be less pronounced.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The magnitude of toughness degradation at cryogenic temperatures is uncertain due to potential contributions from alternative deformation mechanisms (e.g., twinning) that might activate under extreme cooling.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct tensile tests on identical HEA samples at room temperature and at cryogenic temperatures (e.g., -100 °C) while mapping dislocation densities and tracking strain localization via in situ SEM or TEM.
measurements: Uniform elongation and ultimate tensile strength
Strain-hardening curves
Microstructural imaging of dislocation distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the low-temperature samples still exhibit robust dislocation transfer across phase boundaries and maintain ductility comparable to room temperature samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C9

source_paper.title: Interstitial atoms enable joint twinning and transformation induced plasticity in strong and ductile high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: This hypothesis builds on the paper’s observation of nano-carbide formation (PMC5227964::web::005 and ::006) and leverages established principles of carbide-induced grain-boundary embrittlement as seen in conventional alloys (TXT::wikipedia::Segregation_(materials_science)::002 and TXT::wikipedia::Intermetallic::003).
hypotheses.what_is_new: It proposes a deliberate processing modification—extended low-temperature annealing—to induce grain-boundary carbide coarsening within a dual-phase iHEA, thereby triggering a brittle fracture mechanism that contrasts with the uniformly ductile behavior observed under conventional processing.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Extended low‐temperature annealing in the dual‐phase interstitial TWIP–TRIP HEA promotes carbide coarsening and migration to grain boundaries, which in turn reduces grain‐boundary cohesion and induces brittle intergranular fracture.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A dual‐phase interstitial TWIP–TRIP high‐entropy alloy (iHEA) produced via casting, hot‐rolling, homogenization, cold‐rolling, and short-time annealing; it exhibits an f.c.c. γ matrix with dispersed laminate h.c.p. ε phase and uniformly distributed nano‐sized M23C6 carbides predominantly inside grains.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce an extended low‐temperature annealing step (for example, annealing at ~700 °C for an extended duration) after cold‐rolling to stimulate enhanced diffusion of Cr and C and promote the coarsening of nano-carbides and their migration to grain boundaries.
hypothesis.conditions: Annealing parameters should be chosen to maintain the dual‐phase structure while promoting carbide growth at grain boundaries; subsequent room-temperature tensile and fracture toughness testing should replicate service load conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Coarse, brittle M23C6 carbide films along grain boundaries formed by the diffusion‐mediated coalescence of intragranular carbides.
hypothesis.mechanism: At extended low-temperature annealing, enhanced diffusion along grain boundaries causes Cr and carbon to segregate and coalesce into larger, brittle carbide precipitates at grain boundaries. These brittle films reduce intergranular cohesion so that under applied stress, cracks nucleate and propagate along the weakened boundaries, leading to a degradation in toughness.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline standard processing (which yields uniformly distributed nano-carbides), the modified annealed samples will exhibit a significant reduction in toughness (lower fracture toughness and ductility) and a fracture surface with marked intergranular features.
hypothesis.baseline: Dual-phase iHEA processed via standard annealing that yields a uniform intragranular nano-carbide distribution with active TWIP and TRIP mechanisms, leading to high toughness.
hypothesis.boundary: This behavior is expected as long as the annealing treatment promotes carbide coarsening at grain boundaries without triggering complete phase transformation or excessive grain coarsening.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise annealing time and temperature window required to induce significant grain-boundary carbide precipitation without degrading the overall microstructure is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of dual-phase iHEA samples: one following the standard processing route and one with the added extended low-temperature annealing. Characterize the carbide size and location via TEM/EDS, then perform room-temperature tensile tests and fracture toughness measurements. Analyze fracture surfaces with SEM to determine if intergranular features dominate in the modified samples.
measurements: Carbide size and spatial distribution via TEM/EDS
Tensile stress-strain curves including elongation and toughness metrics
SEM fractography to distinguish intergranular versus transgranular fracture features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the extended annealing does not produce increased grain-boundary carbide precipitation or if the mechanical toughness and fracture mode remain statistically similar to that of the standard processed samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.label: C10

source_paper.title: Interstitial atoms enable joint twinning and transformation induced plasticity in strong and ductile high-entropy alloys.

hypotheses.builds_on: This hypothesis extends the findings of the paper regarding the interactions of f.c.c. and h.c.p. phases (PMC5227964::web::009) and applies fracture mechanics principles related to interfacial decohesion (TXT::wikipedia::Fracture_toughness::003) to a cyclic loading regime.
hypotheses.what_is_new: It introduces a novel mechanism where low-temperature cyclic fatigue triggers interphase (f.c.c./h.c.p.) decohesion in a dual-phase HEA, a failure mode that is distinct from conventional grain-boundary embrittlement and not explored in the paper.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Low-temperature cyclic fatigue loading in the dual-phase iHEA promotes interphase decohesion at the f.c.c./h.c.p. interfaces, which leads to premature brittle-like failure under service conditions.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: A dual-phase interstitial TWIP–TRIP HEA with an f.c.c. γ matrix, laminate h.c.p. ε phase, and homogeneously dispersed nano-carbides resulting from standard processing procedures.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject samples to controlled cyclic fatigue loading at a reduced temperature (e.g., around –50 °C) and compare the results with samples deformed under monotonic loading or cyclic loading at room temperature.
hypothesis.conditions: Fatigue tests should be conducted under low-temperature conditions where atomic mobility is reduced, so that any interfacial damage or decohesion between the f.c.c. and h.c.p. phases is more likely to be retained. Loading amplitudes should mimic extreme service conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Decohesion and microcrack initiation along the interfaces between the f.c.c. matrix and the h.c.p. phase.
hypothesis.mechanism: Under cyclic fatigue at low temperatures, the differing mechanical responses of the f.c.c. and h.c.p. phases generate cyclic stresses concentrated at their interfaces. With reduced atomic mobility at low temperature, microdamage and microcracks accumulate along these interphase boundaries without efficient healing. Over multiple cycles, this leads to decohesion at the f.c.c./h.c.p. interfaces, providing preferential sites for brittle crack initiation and propagation.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Samples subjected to low-temperature cyclic fatigue loading will exhibit a lower fatigue life, reduced toughness, and fracture surfaces decorated with signs of interphase decohesion, in contrast to samples tested under room-temperature or monotonic loading conditions.
hypothesis.baseline: Dual-phase iHEA samples deformed under monotonic loading at room temperature, which show active TWIP/TRIP behavior with uniformly distributed deformation mechanisms and ductile fracture characteristics.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate under cyclic loading at sufficiently low temperatures; at higher temperatures or under monotonic loading, the ductile mechanisms observed in the baseline will prevail.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact cyclic strain amplitude and frequency threshold required to trigger significant interphase decohesion in the dual-phase system is not fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare iHEA samples and subject one group to cyclic fatigue loading at –50 °C and another to either room-temperature cyclic loading or monotonic loading. Use TEM/EBSD to analyze the integrity of the f.c.c./h.c.p. interfaces, measure fatigue life via S–N curves, and perform SEM fractography to identify interphase decohesion versus ductile failure.
measurements: Fatigue life (S–N curves) at different temperatures
TEM/EBSD imaging to assess interphase boundary integrity
SEM fractography to determine presence of decohesion along f.c.c./h.c.p. interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If low-temperature cyclic fatigue samples do not display a significantly higher degree of interphase decohesion or reduced fatigue life relative to the control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.
